subject: Ancient History
sub_topic: Spread of Buddhism — India and abroad

concepts.name: Three Buddhist Councils: Chronology, Venues, and Doctrinal Outcomes
key_dimensions: Patron rulers and presiding monks for each council (1st: Ajatashatru/Mahakassapa; 2nd: Kalasoka/Sabakami; 3rd: Ashoka/Moggaliputta Tissa; 4th: Kanishka/Vasumitra)
Doctrinal controversies settled and schisms formalized — especially the Theravada–Mahasanghika split at the 2nd council
UPSC trap: the 4th council is disputed — Theravada tradition does not recognize it; it is associated with Sarvastivada/Mahayana
Outcome texts: Tipitaka compiled at 1st, Abhidhamma Pitaka refined at 3rd, Mahavibhasha at 4th

concepts.name: Ashoka's Role in the Spread of Buddhism: Mechanisms and Geographic Reach
key_dimensions: Dhamma Mahamattas as institutional missionaries — distinct from personal envoys
Rock Edicts and Pillar Edicts as soft-power tools: naming of Hellenistic kings (Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus) in RE XIII
Mission to Sri Lanka (Mahinda/Sanghamitra) vs. missions to Central Asia and the Hellenistic world — different pathways and evidential basis
UPSC trap: Ashoka promoted 'Dhamma,' not Buddhism per se — distinction between personal faith and state policy

concepts.name: Theravada vs. Mahayana: Doctrinal Differences and Geographical Spread
key_dimensions: Bodhisattva ideal (Mahayana) vs. Arahant ideal (Theravada) — implications for missionary outreach
Theravada spread: Sri Lanka → Myanmar → Thailand → Cambodia (southern/southeastern route)
Mahayana spread: Central Asia → China → Korea → Japan (northern/silk road route)
UPSC trap: Vajrayana is a branch of Mahayana, not a separate 'school' on par with Theravada — classification errors are common

concepts.name: Spread of Buddhism to Sri Lanka: Historical Evidence and Significance
key_dimensions: Mahinda's mission — Pali canon as the vehicle; Anuradhapura as the center
Sanghamitra's role: bringing the Bodhi tree sapling — religious symbolism and women's ordination (Bhikkhuni Sangha)
Mahavamsa and Dipavamsa as sources — their reliability and sectarian bias
UPSC trap: Mahinda is traditionally held to be Ashoka's son, but this is debated — some sources call him a monk, not his biological son

concepts.name: Buddhism Along the Silk Road: Trade Networks as Vectors of Religious Spread
key_dimensions: Role of merchant guilds (shrenis) and Kushana patronage in Central Asian spread
Gandhara and Mathura as twin artistic and missionary hubs connecting India to Central Asia
Dunhuang cave networks, Bamiyan Buddhas — material evidence of Silk Road Buddhism
UPSC trap: Buddhism reached China via the Silk Road (overland + maritime), not exclusively overland — the maritime route through Southeast Asia is often overlooked

concepts.name: Kushana Empire and Buddhist Patronage: Kanishka's Contribution
key_dimensions: 4th Buddhist Council under Kanishka — formalization of Sarvastivada and Mahayana texts
Gandhara art school: Greco-Buddhist fusion — anthropomorphic Buddha images (contrast with earlier aniconic tradition)
Kushana coins featuring Buddha — earliest numismatic evidence of Buddha imagery
UPSC trap: Kanishka patronized Buddhism but his coins show multiple deities (Shiva, Mithra, Nana) — he was not exclusively Buddhist

concepts.name: Nalanda and Vikramashila: Universities as Centres of Buddhist Diffusion
key_dimensions: Nalanda's international student body — Chinese (Xuanzang, Yijing), Tibetan, Southeast Asian scholars as evidence of outward reach
Vikramashila's role in Vajrayana/Tantric Buddhism transmission to Tibet — Atisha's mission
Destruction by Bakhtiyar Khilji (1193) — impact on Buddhist knowledge networks in India
UPSC trap: Nalanda was founded by Kumaragupta I (Gupta period), not by Ashoka — a common misattribution

concepts.name: Buddhism in China: Entry Routes, Key Figures, and Sinification
key_dimensions: Traditional date: Emperor Ming of Han (1st century CE) — White Horse Temple (Baima Si) legend
Xuanzang (7th century CE) and Faxian (5th century CE) as reverse missionaries — their records as historical sources for Indian history
Chan (Zen) Buddhism as a Chinese adaptation — Bodhidharma's role
UPSC trap: Faxian visited India during Chandragupta II's reign (Gupta period), while Xuanzang visited during Harsha's reign — conflating their periods is a common error

concepts.name: Buddhism in Southeast Asia: Modes of Transmission and Regional Variations
key_dimensions: Two waves: early Mahayana (1st–7th century CE via trade) and later Theravada revival (11th–13th century from Sri Lanka)
Srivijaya Empire (Sumatra) as a Mahayana Buddhist hub — Yijing's account
Angkor Wat (Cambodia) — initially Hindu, later Theravada — complexity of religious transitions
UPSC trap: Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia follow Theravada today, but their early Buddhism was often Mahayana — the 'always Theravada' assumption is wrong

concepts.name: Buddhism in Tibet: Vajrayana Transmission and Lamaism
key_dimensions: Two waves of transmission: 7th century (Songtsen Gampo, Padmasambhava) and 11th century (Atisha from Vikramashila)
Tibetan Buddhist canon: Kangyur and Tengyur — preservation of Sanskrit texts lost in India
Dalai Lama institution as a political-religious synthesis — origin in 14th–15th century
UPSC trap: Vajrayana is called 'Tantric Buddhism' — it incorporates elements from Shaivism and Shakta traditions, which makes it distinct from orthodox Mahayana

concepts.name: Decline of Buddhism in India: Internal and External Factors
key_dimensions: Internal factors: monasticism detached from laity, ritualization (Vajrayana), absorption into Hinduism (Buddha as Vishnu's avatar)
External factors: Huna invasions (5th–6th century), Turkic raids (Mahmud of Ghazni, Bakhtiyar Khilji destroying monasteries)
Brahmanical revival (Shankaracharya's Advaita) and Bhakti movement drawing away popular support
UPSC trap: Buddhism did not 'suddenly disappear' — it persisted in Pala Bengal/Bihar until the 12th century; the decline was gradual and uneven

concepts.name: Aniconic vs. Iconic Representation of the Buddha: Transition and Significance
key_dimensions: Early aniconic period (Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati): Buddha represented by symbols — footprints, Bodhi tree, wheel, parasol
Transition to iconic imagery: Gandhara (Greco-Roman influence) and Mathura (indigenous) schools produce first Buddha statues simultaneously
UPSC trap: Mathura school predates or is contemporary with Gandhara — the debate on which school was 'first' is unsettled; avoid asserting primacy
Iconographic differences: Gandhara (wavy hair, toga-like robe) vs. Mathura (shaved head, thin robe, Indian features)

concepts.name: Pali Language and Tipitaka: Role in the Preservation and Spread of Theravada Buddhism
key_dimensions: Pali as a Prakrit lingua franca — NOT Buddha's mother tongue (likely Magadhi); choice of Pali was a deliberate missionary decision
Tipitaka structure: Vinaya (monastic rules), Sutta (discourses), Abhidhamma (philosophical analysis)
Pali Text Society (19th century) and its role in modern Buddhist scholarship and revival
UPSC trap: Sanskrit became the vehicle for Mahayana texts, Pali for Theravada — conflating the two canonical languages is a common mistake

concepts.name: Role of Women in the Spread of Buddhism: Bhikkhuni Sangha
key_dimensions: Mahapajapati Gotami — Buddha's stepmother, first bhikkhuni (nun); Buddha's initial reluctance and Ananda's intervention
Sanghamitra's mission to Sri Lanka — institutionalizing the Bhikkhuni order abroad
Decline of the Bhikkhuni order in Theravada countries and its 20th-century revival controversy
UPSC trap: The Bhikkhuni order died out in Theravada Sri Lanka/Southeast Asia by the 11th century — revival requires an unbroken lineage, which remains contested

concepts.name: Ashoka's Dhamma Edicts as Historical Sources for Buddhist Spread
key_dimensions: Rock Edict XIII: names five Hellenistic kings — evidence of diplomatic-missionary outreach to Hellenic world
Minor Rock Edicts vs. Major Rock Edicts — geographic distribution as a map of Ashokan influence
Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts, Greek and Aramaic inscriptions (Kandahar) — multilingual outreach strategy
UPSC trap: Edicts mention 'Dhamma,' not explicitly 'Buddhism' — Ashoka's universalist approach vs. exclusive Buddhist identity

concepts.name: Buddhist Sangha: Organizational Structure as a Vehicle for Spread
key_dimensions: Sangha as the world's oldest democratic institution — decision-making by consensus (uposatha assemblies)
Viharas as nodes of learning, trade, and cultural exchange — not just religious retreats
Dana (lay patronage) system — reciprocal relationship between monks and merchants enabling geographic spread

UPSC trap: The Sangha was initially only for monks; the laity (upasaka/upasika) formed a separate category — the 'Three Jewels' include Sangha, but lay Buddhists are not formally 'Sangha' in original usage

concepts.name: Faxian and Xuanzang: Their Accounts as Sources for Indian History and Buddhist Geography
key_dimensions: Faxian (399–414 CE): visited during Chandragupta II — documents thriving Buddhism in Gangetic plain and Sri Lanka
Xuanzang (629–645 CE): visited during Harsha's reign — detailed account of Nalanda, decline of Buddhism in NW India, vibrant Buddhism in eastern India
Their accounts as corroborating evidence for Gupta and post-Gupta political history
UPSC trap: Yijing (7th century) is a third Chinese pilgrim often forgotten — he focused on Srivijaya and Nalanda; conflating all three pilgrims' details is a frequent error

concepts.name: Mahayana Buddhism and the Bodhisattva Concept: Implications for Missionary Expansion
key_dimensions: Bodhisattva ideal — postponing nirvana to save all beings — inherently outward-looking and missionary in character
Avalokitesvara, Manjushri, Maitreya — key Bodhisattvas and their regional cults (Guanyin in China, Maitreya in Central Asia)
Mahayana's philosophical openness (sunyata, skillful means/upaya) enabled adaptation to local cultures — key to Silk Road success
UPSC trap: Mahayana called Theravada 'Hinayana' (lesser vehicle) pejoratively — Theravadins reject this label; UPSC questions sometimes use 'Hinayana' as if neutral

concepts.name: Buddhism and Trade: The Merchant-Monk Nexus in Geographic Expansion
key_dimensions: Viharas located along trade routes (Ajanta, Ellora, Karle) — not random but strategically placed for merchant rest stops
Merchants as patrons (dana) and as carriers of Buddhist ideas along maritime and overland routes
Buddhist ethics (non-violence, honest dealing) aligned with mercantile interests — ideological compatibility
UPSC trap: Buddhism's spread was NOT only due to royal patronage — the merchant-led diffusion, especially maritime, is equally important and often underweighted in answers

concepts.name: Modern Buddhist Revival: B.R. Ambedkar's Neo-Buddhism and Global Buddhism
key_dimensions: Ambedkar's conversion on October 14, 1956 (Nagpur) — Navayana or 'Neo-Buddhism' as a social reform movement, distinct from traditional schools
Maha Bodhi Society (Anagarika Dharmapala, 1891) — reclamation of Buddhist sites in India and international revival
Bodh Gaya Management Act controversy — control of the Mahabodhi Temple between Hindus and Buddhists
UPSC trap: Ambedkar's Buddhism is considered a 4th vehicle (Navayana) by some scholars — it explicitly rejects karma and rebirth as traditionally understood, making it doctrinally distinct
